cells.tense: Right now what you give and what comes back sit level without a tally, and you can tell.
cells.act: mark the end of it with a plain act
cells.ask: One thing here is already over — a habit, an old arrangement, a favor long since returned. Close it with a single plain act: a note, a shelf cleared, a walk that ends it.
cells.core:
What was out of proportion has been coming back to level, and it shows in you — who you owe, who owes you — before any numbers get run. That's the point of it. Fairness at this stage isn't careful; it's obvious. You give and something comes back, and neither side keeps a receipt. That ease is real and it's yours.

And something is already finished that hasn't been marked. An ending wants honoring here — small, plain, not the biggest one on the list — so the next thing has room to arrive. Close the one that's over, once. Then it stays closed, and the space it leaves is easy to spot. The balance you're holding now is what feeds this; the ending is just what makes room for what's next.
cells.sheetLine: It's level, and one thing still wants its ending.
cells.verb: leveling what's out of proportion until it sits right again
cells.place: the spot where something built on a false floor comes down at once

cells.tense: You're braced for who'll owe you after the next thing falls, writing the ledger before it lands.
cells.act: hold your shape under the weight
cells.ask: Keep your own terms for a week without renegotiating — the same yes, the same no, the same amount you give — and let nobody argue you into a smaller shape.
cells.core:
You can see the thing coming that won't hold, and instead of letting it come, you're doing the math in advance: who owes what when it lands, whose share was short last time. Fairness has turned into bookkeeping. People you care about are starting to read as line items on a sheet written for a week that hasn't happened, and carrying that sheet weighs more than the week itself will.

What steadies this is endurance, not correction. Stay your shape — the terms you actually keep, the amount you actually give — without gripping them and without being talked smaller. Stand in the week's weight without deciding the future inside it. When the tally quiets, the fairness runs itself again, and you'll still have your terms.

cells.tense: You stood at a door where claiming turned against you, and you're still standing there after it closed.
cells.act: do the small practice again, alone, today
cells.ask: Once a day this week, do the smallest practice you keep — alone, ten minutes at most — and ask nothing of it beyond having done it that day.
cells.core:
You can say what's owed to you, plainly, and then let it go unclaimed. Not because you miss the unfairness — you see it fine — but asking still stops short in you, and the moment passes. So you take less, wait longer, let things slide by that shouldn't.

Reaching harder isn't the route. A small practice, done alone and kept, is. That steady light rebuilds the floor under you — the part that knows its own weight without needing proof. One repeat today, another tomorrow if you can. Fairness starts to feel safe in your own hands again, and the asking can wait until it does.

cells.tense: Say nothing's being counted, and a column fills itself in the background anyway.
cells.act: wait until you know which part matters, then begin with that part
cells.ask: When something stings, hold off on the verdict — no story, no ruling, no change to the count — and stay there until it's plain what the sting was actually about.
cells.core:
You'd say you're at peace with all of them, and mean it. Meanwhile a column of names and old slights you didn't plan to keep keeps itself, quietly, running in the back of the day. It isn't that the denial is false. It's that the count stays out of view, so it can't be set down either.

What changes this is a knowing that arrives before the reasoning does. At the moment something stings, stop short of the verdict and wait — ten minutes of not deciding — until it becomes clear which part of it actually matters. Sit with not knowing instead of filling it. That much is enough for the counting to come back under your hand.
cells.sheetLine: You say nothing's being counted. Something is.

attempts.check: The unsupported claims: that the person's past is what made fairness feel dangerous (Too Little kernel — I keep this off the glass entirely, only 'you stay braced' on what they can recognise). That the weighing is disowned (Unacknowledged kernel — I state it as 'you'd say you're not keeping score,' which the person can refuse and still use the ask). The reader could reasonably say 'I don't keep a ledger' in Too Much or 'I know exactly what I'm owed' in Too Little; both asks survive being wrong, since each is one small plain act the person can test in a week regardless. The sentence that serves me more than them: any line picturing the collapse as tidy, so I keep the picture to the thing already over, not the clearing. The ask in Unacknowledged is the person's own act — sitting before changing the count — and it doesn't require the weighing to have been theirs.
